question: What is the defining feature of a Chola temple?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vimana.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Vimana, the tower rising above the sanctum, is the defining feature of a Chola temple (विमान — चोल मंदिर की पहचान)

 

• In the Big Temple at Tanjore, the vimana rises in many receding storeys and dominates the whole complex.

 

• The Cholas carried the Dravidian style of art and architecture to perfection, and most of their temples were dedicated to Shiva.

 

• Other parts such as the ardhamandapa, mahamandapa and Nandimandapa are arranged in front of the vimana.

 

• The distinction between vimana and sikhara is a standard comparison between Dravidian and Nagara temples in questions on Indian architecture.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dravidian temples have a pyramidal vimana, whereas Nagara temples have a curvilinear shikhara.

 

• Gopurams (gateway towers) became more important in later Pandya and Vijayanagara temples.

 

• Chola bronzes like the Nataraja are another hallmark.

 

• Tall gateway towers (gopurams) became the dominant feature only in later Pandya and Vijayanagara temples, whereas the Chola complex was dominated by the central vimana.

 

NOTE

 

• Stupa (Option 1): A stupa is a Buddhist dome-shaped relic mound, as at Sanchi. It is not a feature of a Shaiva Chola temple, so it fails as the defining element.

 

• Chaitya arch (Option 2): A chaitya arch is the horseshoe-shaped window motif of Buddhist cave halls. It marks early Buddhist architecture and not the Chola temple tradition.

 

• Sikhara (Option 4): A sikhara is the curvilinear tower of northern Nagara temples such as those of Khajuraho. The Chola equivalent is the pyramidal vimana, so this option points to the wrong style.

question:
Assertion (A): The Dravidian style of architecture reached perfection under the Cholas.

Reason (R): The Big Temple at Tanjore, built by Rajaraja I, is a masterpiece of South Indian art and architecture.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true but R is false
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are true and the reason supports the assertion: the Big Temple at Tanjore by Rajaraja I is a masterpiece showing the Dravidian style at its peak (द्रविड़ शैली — चोलकाल में पराकाष्ठा)

 

• The temple combines the vimana, ardhamandapa, mahamandapa and Nandimandapa in a grand design.

 

• The perfection of the style is shown by the scale of the vimana and the careful planning of the whole complex.

 

• It is therefore the best single illustration of why Chola architecture is said to have perfected the style.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Chola bronzes, especially Nataraja, show the same artistic peak.

 

• The temple was built in 1010 AD.

 

• Later Chola temples include Airavateswara at Darasuram.

 

• The same Dravidian tradition continued in the Pallava, Chola and Vijayanagara phases, and the Chola phase is regarded as its classical peak.

 

• Dravidian temples are recognised by their pyramidal vimana over the sanctum, while Nagara temples have a beehive-shaped tower, and a third mixed form is called Vesara.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): Choosing the option that R is not the explanation is wrong because the Tanjore temple is exactly the evidence that is cited for the perfection of the style. R therefore explains A.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 3): Calling A true and R false is wrong, since the notes call the Tanjore temple a masterpiece and name Rajaraja I as the builder. R is accurate.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): Declaring A false is wrong because the notes state that the Dravidian style reached perfection under the Cholas. Both statements are true.

question: The bronze statues of which deity are regarded as masterpieces of Chola art?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Nataraja, the dancing Shiva.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The bronze statues of Nataraja, the dancing Shiva, are masterpieces of Chola art (नटराज की कांस्य मूर्तियाँ — चोल कला की उत्कृष्ट कृतियाँ)

 

• Chola bronzes were cast by the lost-wax (cire perdue) method and were made for temple worship and processions.

 

• The popularity of Nataraja images fits the fact that most Chola temples were dedicated to Shiva.

 

• Along with temple architecture, these bronzes are the finest artistic legacy of the dynasty.

 

• The Nataraja form expresses the cosmic dance of Shiva and became the symbol most closely linked with South Indian temple art and philosophy.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Chola Nataraja bronzes are known worldwide for their dynamic poise.

 

• The Chola kings were largely Shaiva devotees.

 

• Chola temple walls also carried detailed inscriptions recording grants.

 

• Many bronze images were cast for processions and festivals, and the Chola temples still use some of them in their rituals today.

 

• The Nataraja bronze usually shows Shiva dancing within a ring of flames with one foot on a small figure that stands for ignorance.

 

NOTE

 

• Vishnu as Varaha (Option 2): Varaha images appear in the Gupta and early Chalukya sculptures, such as the Udayagiri boar. It is not the deity for which Chola bronze work is mainly celebrated.

 

• Buddha in meditation (Option 3): Buddha statues are the hallmark of the Gandhara and Mathura schools and of Gupta Sarnath. The Chola bronze tradition was Shaiva, so this is not what the notes highlight.

 

• Durga Mahishasuramardini (Option 4): Durga Mahishasuramardini is a famous sculptural theme at Mamallapuram of the Pallava period. It is a stone relief and not the Chola bronze masterpiece the question refers to.

question: Which Chola ruler took the title 'Gangaikonda Chola', meaning 'Conqueror of the Ganga'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rajendra I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rajendra I took the title Gangaikonda Chola, 'Conqueror of the Ganga', after his successful northern campaign (गंगैकोंड चोल — राजेंद्र प्रथम की उपाधि)

 

• To mark this triumph he founded the city of Gangaikondacholapuram and made it his capital.

 

• He ruled from 1012 to 1044 AD, so the title belongs to the peak of Chola power.

 

• The same city has a Siva temple built by Rajendra I, listed among the great Chola monuments.

 

• The title shows that the Chola ruler wanted to place himself on a level with the great northern conquerors who had marched to the Ganga.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• His northern march reportedly reached the Ganga region and defeated the Pala king Mahipala I.

 

• He also dug the Cholagangam tank near his capital.

 

• He was the son of Rajaraja I.

 

• The Chola king reportedly brought water from the Ganga to his capital, which is said to be the reason for creating the large tank called Cholagangam.

 

NOTE

 

• Rajaraja I (Option 1): Rajaraja I was the father of Rajendra I and built the Brihadeshwara temple at Tanjore. He is remembered as the greatest Chola builder but not as Gangaikonda.

 

• Aditya I (Option 2): Aditya I belonged to the early Imperial Chola kings and helped end Pallava power in the late 9th century. He lived well before the northern campaign that earned the title.

 

• Kulottunga I (Option 4): Kulottunga I came to the throne in 1070 AD, after the peak of Chola power, and is remembered for abolishing tolls. The title Gangaikonda is not his.

question:
Consider the following statements about Rajendra I:

1. He founded the city of Gangaikondacholapuram and made it his capital.

2. He dug a large irrigation tank called Cholagangam on the western side of the city.

3. He built the Brihadeshwara temple at Tanjore in 1010 AD.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Claims 1 and 2 hold true: Rajendra I founded Gangaikondacholapuram as his capital and dug the Cholagangam tank to its west (राजेंद्र प्रथम — गंगैकोंडचोलपुरम, चोलगंगम तालाब)

 

• Claim 3 fails because the Brihadeshwara temple at Tanjore was built by his father Rajaraja I.

 

• The new capital commemorated his northern campaign and the title Gangaikonda Chola.

 

• The tank served as an irrigation work, which is why a recent SSC key credits Rajendra I with Chola irrigation development.

 

• The tank and the new capital together illustrate how Chola kings combined military conquest with public works in the Kaveri region.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Cholagangam tank is known in Tamil as Chola Gangam eri.

 

• Rajendra I ruled from 1012 to 1044 AD.

 

• His capital also has a Siva temple built by him.

 

• The Cholagangam tank was an enormous work meant for irrigation, and it is sometimes counted among the great artificial lakes of its time.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Only 2 and 3 accepts the false claim that Rajendra I built the Tanjore Big Temple. The temple was built by Rajaraja I, and statement 1 is true as well, so this fails.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): Only 1 and 3 includes the same false temple claim and leaves out the irrigation tank. Since statement 2 is correct and statement 3 is wrong, this combination cannot stand.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): 1, 2 and 3 would be correct only if the Tanjore temple were Rajendra's work. It is the work of his father, so adding statement 3 makes the answer wrong.

question: The Chola navy under Rajendra I launched a famous overseas expedition against the Srivijaya kingdom. Srivijaya was located in:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Southeast Asia.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Srivijaya empire lay in Southeast Asia, with its centre in Sumatra, and was attacked by the Chola fleet under Rajendra I (श्रीविजय — दक्षिण-पूर्व एशिया, चोल नौसेना का अभियान)

 

• The expedition, usually dated about 1025 AD, is the best-known example of the Chola naval power in the Indian Ocean.

 

• Srivijaya controlled the sea lanes of the Malacca Strait, which were vital for trade between India and China.

 

• The campaign shows that the empire's reach extended beyond the peninsula under its two greatest rulers.

 

• The overseas campaign is the main reason historians describe the Cholas as one of the few Indian dynasties to have used naval power on such a scale.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Cholas also conquered northern Sri Lanka and the Maldives under Rajaraja I.

 

• The Chola navy used the east-coast ports for such voyages.

 

• Chola trade links extended to China and Southeast Asia.

 

• The Chola navy also influenced the spread of Indian culture in Southeast Asia, where Tamil merchant guilds were active in the 11th and 12th centuries.

 

NOTE

 

• East Africa (Option 1): East Africa was reached by Arab and Indian traders but was never a target of Chola fleets. The Chola dynasty is not known for any expedition in that direction.

 

• Arabia (Option 2): Arabia was part of the Arab trading world to the west, with which the Cholas had trade contacts but no warlike expedition. Srivijaya was not located there.

 

• Central Asia (Option 3): Central Asia is a landlocked region and could not be reached by a naval expedition. The Chola navy operated in the Indian Ocean and Bay of Bengal, not there.

question:
Consider the following statements about Rajaraja I:

1. He ruled from 985 to 1014 AD.

2. He built the Brihadeshwara temple at Tanjore in 1010 AD.

3. He took the title Gangaikonda Chola.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Items 1 and 2 are right: Rajaraja I ruled 985-1014 AD and built the Brihadeshwara temple in 1010 AD (राजराज प्रथम — 985-1014 ई., बृहदीश्वर मंदिर)

 

• Claim 3 goes wrong since the title Gangaikonda Chola was taken by his son Rajendra I after the northern campaign.

 

• Under Rajaraja I the Chola kingdom grew into an empire that included northern Sri Lanka and much of South India.

 

• His reign and his son's together mark the highest point of Chola power.

 

• The distinction between the father and son is crucial, because most of the confusion in questions arises from giving the same title to both rulers.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• He annexed northern Sri Lanka and made it a Chola province.

 

• The temple is dedicated to Shiva and is also called Rajarajeswara.

 

• Rajendra I was the next ruler, and the two ruled jointly for a short period.

 

• Rajaraja I also conquered the Maldives and annexed northern Sri Lanka, whose capital Anuradhapura was ruined during his campaigns.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Only 2 and 3 wrongly gives the Gangaikonda title to Rajaraja I. The title came to Rajendra I, and statement 1 on his dates is also true, so this combination fails.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): Only 1 and 3 accepts the false title claim and ignores the correct temple statement. The temple at Tanjore is the best known work of Rajaraja I, so dropping it is an error.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): 1, 2 and 3 fails because statement 3 is not true of Rajaraja. His son Rajendra I took the name Gangaikonda, so the full set cannot be correct.

question: Who was the last Chola king, defeated by Jatavarman Sundara Pandya II, after which the Chola country was absorbed into the Pandya Empire?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rajendra III.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rajendra III was the last Chola king; he was defeated by Jatavarman Sundara Pandya II and the Chola country was then absorbed into the Pandya Empire (राजेंद्र तृतीय — अंतिम चोल शासक)

 

• The Pandyas had been a Sangam-age power and revived in the 13th century to end the long Chola rule.

 

• With this defeat the line of Imperial Cholas, begun by Vijayalaya, came to a close.

 

• The decline had begun after the great days of Rajaraja I and Rajendra I.

 

• The end of the Cholas came after a long period of decline, during which feudatories grew powerful and the Pandyas gained strength in the south.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Cholas rose in the 9th century and ended in the 13th century.

 

• The Pandya capital was Madurai.

 

• The fish (carp) was the Pandya emblem.

 

• Jatavarman Sundara Pandya II belonged to the Second Pandya Empire, which flourished in the 13th century with Madurai as its capital.

 

• After the fall of the Cholas, the Pandya empire under rulers such as Jatavarman Sundara Pandya II became the strongest power in the far south for a time.

 

NOTE

 

• Kulottunga III (Option 1): Kulottunga III was a late Chola ruler who is linked with the Kampaharesvara temple at Tribhuvanam. He came before the last king, so he was not the ruler defeated by Jatavarman Sundara Pandya II.

 

• Rajadhiraja I (Option 2): Rajadhiraja I ruled in the 11th century, when the Cholas were still powerful, and fought the Western Chalukyas. He lived about two centuries before the fall of the dynasty.

 

• Aditya I (Option 3): Aditya I was a 9th-century ruler who helped establish the imperial Chola line by ending Pallava power. He belongs to the beginning of the dynasty and not its end.

question: Arrange the following Chola rulers in chronological order (earliest first): 1. Rajendra III 2. Vijayalaya 3. Rajendra I 4. Rajaraja I
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2, 4, 3, 1.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct order is Vijayalaya (9th century), Rajaraja I (985-1014), Rajendra I (1012-1044) and Rajendra III (the last king) (विजयालय → राजराज I → राजेंद्र I → राजेंद्र III)

 

• Vijayalaya founded the Imperial line, so he comes first, and Rajendra III as the last ruler comes last.

 

• Rajaraja I preceded his son Rajendra I, who succeeded and extended his empire.

 

• This sequence follows the rise, peak and fall of the Chola empire: founding, expansion, northern conquests and finally defeat by the Pandyas.

 

• Arranging rulers by date is easier if one recalls the sequence of founding, peak under father and son, decline and final absorption by the Pandyas.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rajendra I was the son of Rajaraja I.

 

• Rajendra III was defeated by Jatavarman Sundara Pandya II.

 

• Gangaikondacholapuram became the capital under Rajendra I.

 

• A simple memory aid for this order is founder first, then the father and son at the peak, and the last king at the end.

 

• Aditya I, Parantaka I and Kulottunga I also belong to the Chola list and often appear as options in similar sequencing questions.

 

NOTE

 

• 2, 3, 4, 1 (Option 1): The sequence 2, 3, 4, 1 puts Rajendra I before his father Rajaraja I. Since the son succeeded the father, this order is reversed in the middle.

 

• 4, 2, 3, 1 (Option 3): The sequence 4, 2, 3, 1 places Rajaraja I before the founder Vijayalaya. The founder lived in the 9th century, long before the king of the 10th-11th centuries.

 

• 2, 4, 1, 3 (Option 4): The sequence 2, 4, 1, 3 places Rajendra III before Rajendra I. The first Rajendra reigned at the peak, whereas the third was the last ruler of the declining dynasty.

question: Which of the following was NOT a Chola ruler?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Narasimhavarman I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla) was a Pallava ruler of Kanchipuram who built the Seven Rathas at Mamallapuram, not a Chola (नरसिंहवर्मन प्रथम — पल्लव शासक)

 

• The Chola rulers in the list are Vijayalaya (founder of the imperial line), Rajaraja I and Rajendra I.

 

• The Pallavas were the early overlords of the Cholas, since Vijayalaya is believed to have been a Pallava feudatory.

 

• Pallava rule belongs to the chapter on regional South Indian dynasties.

 

• The Pallavas and the Cholas were two different dynasties of the Tamil region, and the Cholas rose to power partly at the expense of the Pallavas.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• An SSC key credits Narasimhavarman I with the Seven Rathas of Mahabalipuram.

 

• Mahendravarman I carried titles like Vichitrachitta.

 

• Mamallapuram is a UNESCO site.

 

• Pallava Narasimhavarman I defeated the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II in the 7th century, so he belongs to an entirely different dynastic story.

 

• The Pallavas ruled from Kanchipuram, and the Seven Rathas of Mamallapuram, built under Narasimhavarman I, are often asked in the same group of questions.

 

NOTE

 

• Vijayalaya (Option 1): Vijayalaya was the founder of the Imperial Chola line in the 9th century and is clearly a Chola ruler. He cannot be the odd one out in this question.

 

• Rajaraja I (Option 2): Rajaraja I of 985-1014 AD was a Chola king who built the Brihadeshwara temple. As a Chola monarch he does not fit the NOT-type requirement.

 

• Rajendra I (Option 3): Rajendra I of 1012-1044 AD was the Chola king titled Gangaikonda Chola. Since he is a Chola ruler, he is not the exception.

question: What does 'Ur' refer to in the context of Chola village administration?
solution_text:
The correct answer is The assembly of common people.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ur was the assembly of common people in Chola village administration (ऊर — सामान्य जनों की ग्राम सभा)

 

• It functioned alongside the Sabha, which was the assembly of Brahmins in Brahmadeya villages.

 

• These bodies gave the Chola villages a high degree of local self-government, handling matters such as land, irrigation and temples.

 

• The Uttaramerur inscription is the best-known record of village administration under the Cholas.

 

• The Ur and the Sabha together show that Chola villages had separate institutions for different groups, a feature that impressed later historians.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ur and Sabha together show the two-tier social base of Chola village life.

 

• Land granted to temples was called Devadana.

 

• A village organisation of this kind was an important feature of Chola governance.

 

• The Chola kings had also other village bodies, such as the committees that looked after tanks, gardens and temple affairs in each settlement.

 

NOTE

 

• An assembly of Brahmins (Option 1): An assembly of Brahmins was called the Sabha, not Ur. Brahmin-dominated villages (brahmadeya) were run by it, so this option mixes up the two assemblies.

 

• A tax collector (Option 2): A tax collector is an official, whereas Ur was a collective body of villagers. The Chola tax terms in the notes include Vetti, a forced labour tax, not Ur.

 

• A land grant to temples (Option 4): A land grant to temples was known as Devadana. Ur was the village assembly and has nothing to do with the type of land donation.

question:
Consider the following statements about Chola local self-government:

1. Ur was the assembly of common people.

2. Sabha was the assembly of Brahmins.

3. Vetti was a tax paid in grain.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Ur was the assembly of common people and Sabha the assembly of Brahmins (ऊर और सभा — चोल ग्राम प्रशासन की संस्थाएँ)

 

• Statement 3 is wrong because Vetti was a form of forced labour tax, not a payment in grain.

 

• Grain payments are linked with the land revenue known as kadamai, which is a different tax.

 

• These bodies were responsible for the management of villages, giving the Chola system its reputation for local autonomy.

 

• The Chola village bodies are often called an early form of local self-government, though their membership was limited by caste and property.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Brahmadeya villages were granted to Brahmans.

 

• The Chola land revenue was collected as a share of produce.

 

• Local assemblies kept village records.

 

• Forced labour taxes of the Vetti type were common in medieval South India, and the temple as well as the state could demand them.

 

• Records of the Chola villages were kept on temple walls, and the local assemblies had committees to supervise tanks, gardens, justice and temple funds.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Only 2 and 3 includes the false claim about Vetti. A forced-labour tax cannot be a payment in grain, and the statement about Ur is true, so this combination fails.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): Only 1 and 3 repeats the wrong statement 3 and omits the Sabha statement. Because the Sabha was the Brahmin assembly, statement 2 should be included.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): 1, 2 and 3 is wrong because statement 3 is false. Vetti was labour service demanded by the state or the temple, not a tax collected as grain.

question: The Uttaramerur inscription gives valuable information about which aspect of the Chola rule?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Village administration.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Uttaramerur inscription tells us about village administration under the Chola dynasty, including how the village assemblies worked (उत्तरमेरूर अभिलेख — चोलकालीन ग्राम प्रशासन)

 

• It reveals a system of local self-government with the Sabha and Ur managing local affairs.

 

• Uttaramerur is a village in Tamil Nadu, and its inscriptions are carved on the walls of a temple.

 

• Such inscriptions are regarded as among the best epigraphic sources for Indian rural institutions.

 

• The inscription is carved on temple walls, which shows that the temple was also the place where public records were displayed to the community.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The inscriptions mention the election of members by a system using palm-leaf tickets drawn from a pot (kudavolai).

 

• Records of this kind dating to the time of Parantaka I are famous.

 

• The Cholas kept careful inscriptional records of grants.

 

• Uttaramerur is in the Kanchipuram region of Tamil Nadu, and its inscriptions are dated to the reign of the Chola king Parantaka I.

 

NOTE

 

• Naval expeditions to Southeast Asia (Option 1): Naval expeditions to Southeast Asia are known from the records of Rajendra I and the Srivijaya campaign, not from Uttaramerur. This inscription is a record of local village matters.

 

• Temple building techniques (Option 2): Temple building techniques are best studied from the monuments themselves, such as the Big Temple at Tanjore. The Uttaramerur inscription is not a technical treatise on construction.

 

• Foreign trade with Rome (Option 3): Foreign trade with Rome belongs to the Sangam age and is described in Sangam poems and classical accounts. The Uttaramerur inscription is not a source for that commerce.

question:
Consider the following types of Chola land donations:

1. Brahmadeya - land given to Brahmans

2. Devadana - land given to temples

3. Pallichchhandam - land given to the Jain community

Which of the above pairs is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• All three pairs are correct: Brahmadeya (Brahmans), Devadana (temples) and Pallichchhandam (Jain community) (ब्रह्मदेय, देवदान, पल्लिच्चंदम् — चोलकालीन भूमि अनुदान)

 

• These grants show how the Chola state used land to support religious and social institutions.

 

• Other types in the notes include Vellanvagai (land for non-Brahmans and peasants) and Shalabhoga (land for a school).

 

• Brahmadeya villages were usually run by the Sabha of Brahmins.

 

• Land grants were a major way in which the Chola state rewarded Brahmans, supported temples and encouraged the spread of agriculture.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pallichchhandam is derived from the word 'palli' used for Jain establishments.

 

• Land revenue in the Chola kingdom was called kadamai.

 

• Vellanvagai land was held by peasants and non-Brahmans.

 

• The notes list five types of Chola land grants, and the names Vellanvagai and Shalabhoga are the least known and so most often asked.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): Only 1 and 2 omits the Jain grant, which is a correct pair. Pallichchhandam did mean land given to the Jain community, so excluding it makes this option incomplete.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Only 2 and 3 omits the Brahmin grant, also a correct pair. Brahmadeya meant land given to Brahmans, so the answer must include statement 1.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 4): Only 1 and 3 omits the Devadana pair. Land gifted to temples was known as Devadana, so leaving it out makes the option incomplete.

question: In the Chola empire, land granted for the maintenance of a school was known as:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shalabhoga.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Shalabhoga was the land given for the upkeep of a school under the Cholas (शालाभोग — विद्यालय के रखरखाव हेतु भूमि)

 

• It shows that the Chola state and donors supported education through land endowments, often attached to temples.

 

• The Cholas had a developed system of land grants, each with a separate name based on the recipient.

 

• Other grants included Brahmadeya, Devadana, Vellanvagai and Pallichchhandam.

 

• The existence of a separate grant for schools shows that education in the Chola period was supported by the endowments of donors and the state.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Vellanvagai was land for non-Brahmans and peasants.

 

• Many Chola temples also functioned as centres of learning.

 

• Land grants were recorded in copper plates and stone inscriptions.

 

• Schools and colleges attached to temples taught the Vedas and grammar, and were supported by the revenue of lands specially granted.

 

• Gifts to temples and schools were recorded in inscriptions, and many such records name the donors, the lands given and the purpose of the gift.

 

NOTE

 

• Pallichchhandam (Option 2): Pallichchhandam was land given to the Jain community for its institutions. It supported religious establishments of another faith and not a school.

 

• Brahmadeya (Option 3): Brahmadeya was land given to Brahmans, often forming whole villages run by their Sabha. It benefited a class of scholars but did not mean a school grant.

 

• Devadana (Option 4): Devadana was land given to temples for worship and maintenance. Though temples sometimes ran schools, this name refers to a temple's holding and not school upkeep.

question:
Match the type of Chola land grant with its recipient.

a. Brahmadeya

b. Vellanvagai

c. Devadana

d. Shalabhoga

i. Temples

ii. Brahmans

iii. A school

iv. Non-Brahmans and peasants
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct match is Brahmadeya - Brahmans, Vellanvagai - non-Brahmans and peasants, Devadana - temples, Shalabhoga - a school (ब्रह्मदेय, वेल्लानवगै, देवदान, शालाभोग)

 

• The names tell the purpose: 'deya' means gift, 'deva' means god, and 'shala' means school.

 

• These grants formed the base of Chola religious and educational institutions and rural society.

 

• Pallichchhandam, the grant to the Jain community, is the fifth type listed in the notes.

 

• The names of the grants are easy to recall if one connects each with its recipient: Brahmans, temples, peasants and the school.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Brahmadeya villages had the Sabha as their assembly.

 

• Ur was the assembly of common people.

 

• Land revenue was known as kadamai.

 

• A fifth grant, Pallichchhandam, supported the Jain community, which shows that the Chola state also gave support to faiths other than Shaivism.

 

• Pallichchhandam grants to Jains are a useful reminder that the Chola kings, though mainly Shaiva, also supported other religious communities in their kingdom.

 

NOTE

 

• a-i, b-iv, c-ii, d-iii (Option 1): a-i, b-iv, c-ii, d-iii swaps the temple and Brahman grants. Devadana was for temples and Brahmadeya for Brahmans, so two of its four pairs are wrong.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii (Option 2): a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii pairs Vellanvagai with temples and Devadana with non-Brahmans. Vellanvagai was for peasants and Devadana for temples, so it also confuses two entries.

 

• a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i (Option 4): a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i gives all four wrong recipients. Shalabhoga did not go to temples and Devadana was not for a school, so none of its pairs is accurate.

question: In what form was the 'Vetti' tax collected during the Chola period?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Forced labour.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Vetti was a form of forced labour tax in the Chola period (वेट्टि — बेगार या जबरन श्रम के रूप में कर)

 

• People rendered unpaid service for work such as building and repairing temples, tanks and roads instead of paying in cash or kind.

 

• It is one of the taxes named in the notes under Chola administration.

 

• The state's main land revenue, in contrast, is known as kadamai.

 

• Forced labour was an important source of workers for large Chola projects such as irrigation tanks, canals and temple construction.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The word Vetti is still used in Tamil for unpaid labour.

 

• Chola irrigation tanks needed constant labour, which the system supplied.

 

• Other terms: Brahmadeya, Devadana, Shalabhoga.

 

• The Chola state also collected taxes on trade, on professions and on land, and most were paid in kind or in gold coins.

 

• A famous terms list for the Chola economy includes vetti for labour, kadamai for land revenue, and devadana for gifts to temples.

 

NOTE

 

• Cash (Option 1): Cash payment was used for several levies and for trade, but Vetti was not a monetary tax. It was labour service, so cash does not describe it.

 

• Gold (Option 3): Gold was a form of high-value payment and gifts, but the Vetti burden fell on common villagers who could provide only their labour. It was not collected as gold.

 

• Grain (Option 4): Grain was the usual form in which land revenue (kadamai) was paid by cultivators. Vetti was different, since it required work and not produce.

question:
Consider the following statements about Chola taxes and land:

1. Vetti was a form of forced labour tax.

2. Kadamai was the term for land revenue in the Chola kingdom.

3. Shalabhoga was land given to temples.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Vetti was a forced labour tax and Kadamai was the land revenue term (वेट्टि और कदमै — चोलकालीन कर)

 

• Statement 3 is wrong because land given to temples was Devadana, whereas Shalabhoga was for a school.

 

• Land revenue was the chief source of income for the Chola state, collected from cultivators on the produce of their fields.

 

• The distinction between taxes and grants is an easy way to score marks in SSC questions.

 

• The chief land revenue was a share of the produce, and it was supplemented by various other levies and by labour services.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• A similar SSC question has asked which term meant land revenue.

 

• Pallichchhandam was land for Jains.

 

• Brahmadeya was land for Brahmans.

 

• The most common land revenue was kadamai, and the notes give Vetti as the best example of labour taxes in the empire.

 

• Brahmadeya and Devadana lands were often exempt from regular revenue, which meant the state gave up income in return for religious merit.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Only 2 and 3 includes the false claim on Shalabhoga. It was a school grant, not a temple grant, and the Vetti statement is true, so this combination is not valid.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): Only 1 and 3 repeats the wrong Shalabhoga claim and ignores the correct statement on kadamai. Land revenue was kadamai, so this option fails on two counts.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): 1, 2 and 3 fails because statement 3 mixes up two land grants. Devadana was for temples and Shalabhoga for schools, so the set cannot be fully correct.

question:
Match the Chola temple with its builder.

a. Brihadeshwara Temple, Tanjore

b. Siva temple at Gangaikondacholapuram

c. Airavateswara Temple, Darasuram

d. Kampaharesvara Temple, Tribhuvanam

i. Rajendra I

ii. Rajaraja II

iii. Rajaraja I

iv. Kulottunga III
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct match is Brihadeshwara - Rajaraja I, Gangaikondacholapuram - Rajendra I, Airavateswara - Rajaraja II, Kampaharesvara - Kulottunga III (तंजावुर, गंगैकोंडचोलपुरम, दारासुरम, तिरुभुवनम् मंदिर)

 

• The first three builders and temples come directly from the notes, and Kampaharesvara is given as a later Chola example.

 

• The sequence tracks Chola art from its early grandeur to its late phase, all in the Dravidian style.

 

• Kulottunga III is the late Chola king associated with the Tribhuvanam temple.

 

• A match question on temples is best solved by first fixing the father-son pair, which are Rajaraja I at Tanjore and Rajendra I at his new capital.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Brihadeshwara and Gangaikondacholapuram temples are both Siva temples.

 

• Darasuram's temple is known for its fine sculpture.

 

• These sites are part of the Great Living Chola Temples.

 

• The temples at Tanjore, Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram are today grouped together as the Great Living Chola Temples by UNESCO.

 

• The Brihadeshwara temple is nearly 66 metres tall and is built of granite, whereas the temple at Darasuram is smaller but famous for its sculpture.

 

NOTE

 

• a-i, b-iii, c-ii, d-iv (Option 1): a-i, b-iii, c-ii, d-iv swaps the first two builders. The Tanjore temple was built by Rajaraja I and the Gangaikondacholapuram one by his son Rajendra I, so two pairs are wrong.

 

• a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii (Option 2): a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii swaps the last two. Darasuram is linked with Rajaraja II and Tribhuvanam with Kulottunga III, so it fails.

 

• a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv (Option 4): a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv misassigns the first three temples completely. Only the last pair is correct, so most of the match is wrong.

question:
Match the Chola ruler with the event or achievement.

a. Vijayalaya

b. Rajaraja I

c. Rajendra I

d. Rajendra III

i. Took the title Gangaikonda Chola

ii. Last Chola king

iii. Built the Big Temple at Tanjore

iv. Founded the Imperial Chola line
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct match is Vijayalaya - founded the Imperial line, Rajaraja I - Big Temple, Rajendra I - Gangaikonda title, Rajendra III - last king (विजयालय, राजराज, राजेंद्र प्रथम, राजेंद्र तृतीय)

 

• The four rulers cover the beginning, peak and end of the Imperial Chola dynasty.

 

• The Big Temple was completed in 1010 AD and Rajendra I's title followed his northern campaign.

 

• Rajendra III was defeated by Jatavarman Sundara Pandya II, and the Chola country merged with the Pandya empire.

 

• The pairs also reveal the shape of Chola history, with a founder, two great conquerors and a last king defeated by the Pandyas.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rajaraja I ruled 985-1014 AD, and Rajendra I 1012-1044 AD.

 

• Vijayalaya is believed to have been a Pallava feudatory.

 

• Gangaikondacholapuram was the new capital founded by Rajendra I.

 

• Rajendra III was the last of the Imperial Cholas, and his defeat marked the end of the line begun by Vijayalaya four centuries earlier.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii (Option 1): a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii gives the Big Temple to Vijayalaya and the founding of the line to Rajaraja I. The founder and builder are reversed, so the first two pairs are wrong.

 

• a-iv, b-i, c-iii, d-ii (Option 3): a-iv, b-i, c-iii, d-ii swaps the achievements of the two great kings. The title Gangaikonda belongs to Rajendra I and the Tanjore temple to Rajaraja I.

 

• a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv (Option 4): a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv calls Vijayalaya the last king and Rajendra III the founder. That reverses the dynasty's timeline and is wrong.

question:
Assertion (A): Rajendra I founded the city of Gangaikondacholapuram and made it his capital.

Reason (R): He wished to mark his successful campaign in the north, which earned him the title Gangaikonda Chola.
option_1: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true but R is false
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are true and R explains A: Rajendra I founded Gangaikondacholapuram to commemorate his northern campaign and took the title Gangaikonda Chola (गंगैकोंडचोलपुरम — राजेंद्र प्रथम की उत्तरी विजय का स्मारक)

 

• The city's name itself means 'the city of the Chola who conquered the Ganga'.

 

• The new capital had a grand Siva temple and the large Cholagangam tank for irrigation.

 

• Hence the founding of the city is directly linked with the victory mentioned in the reason.

 

• The city and the title go together, so any question on one of them can be answered by remembering the other.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Chola kings changed their capitals from Uraiyur and Puhar to Thanjavur and later Gangaikondacholapuram.

 

• The notes call the city his capital after the campaign.

 

• Rajendra I's rule lasted from 1012 to 1044 AD.

 

• The capital stayed at the new city for several generations, and its Siva temple remains a major example of late imperial Chola art.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 2): Saying R does not explain A is wrong because the notes explicitly say the city was founded to mark the northern campaign. The reason gives the cause of the founding.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 3): Treating R as false is wrong because the notes confirm R: the title Gangaikonda Chola means Conqueror of Ganga after the campaign.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): Rejecting A while accepting R is wrong because the notes clearly say Rajendra I founded Gangaikondacholapuram and made it his capital.

question:
Assertion (A): In Chola villages, Ur was the assembly of Brahmins.

Reason (R): Sabha was the assembly of common people.
option_1: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_3: Both A and R are false
option_4: A is true but R is false
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are false.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are false: in fact Ur was the assembly of common people and the Sabha was the assembly of Brahmins (ऊर — आम लोगों की सभा; सभा — ब्राह्मणों की सभा)

 

• The assertion and the reason have simply swapped the two bodies' membership.

 

• Brahmadeya villages, granted to Brahmans, were managed by the Sabha.

 

• The Uttaramerur inscription is the standard source on Chola village administration.

 

• Reversing the roles of the two assemblies is a common trap, so the student should remember that Brahmin villages were governed by the Sabha.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Chola local self-government is among the most-praised features of the dynasty.

 

• Another body existed for merchants in towns.

 

• Learn the pair as Ur-common people and Sabha-Brahmins.

 

• Learning the pairing Ur with the common people and Sabha with Brahmans avoids confusion in both statement and assertion-reason questions.

 

• A separate group of merchants called the Nagaram managed town affairs, while the Ur and the Sabha looked after the village settlements.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A (Option 1): The option that A and R are both true is wrong, because neither is correct. The Ur included ordinary villagers and the Sabha comprised Brahmans, which reverses both statements.

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 2): The option that R correctly explains A fails, since the assertion itself is false. The Sabha was not the common people's body, so no explanation is possible.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 4): The option that A is true but R is false is wrong because the assertion is also incorrect. Only a reversal of the two terms would make the sentences true.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Airavateswara Temple at Darasuram:

1. It was built by Rajaraja II.

2. It is located in the Tanjore region of Tamil Nadu.

3. It is dedicated to Lord Vishnu.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the Airavateswara Temple at Darasuram, Tanjore, was built by Rajaraja II (ऐरावतेश्वर मंदिर, दारासुरम — राजराज द्वितीय)

 

• Statement 3 is wrong because it is a Shaiva temple, dedicated to Shiva as Airavateswara, like most Chola temples.

 

• The name recalls the myth of Indra's white elephant Airavata, which is said to have worshipped Shiva here.

 

• It comes in the later Chola phase, after the great temples of Rajaraja I and Rajendra I.

 

• The temple's name connects it with Indra's elephant Airavata, and its rich carving makes it a favourite subject for art history questions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Darasuram is near Kumbakonam in the Kaveri delta.

 

• The temple is part of the Great Living Chola Temples group.

 

• Most Chola temples were dedicated to Shiva.

 

• Darasuram's temple is known for carved pillars and panels, including a small set of stone steps that produce musical notes when struck.

 

• The temple was built in the 12th century by Rajaraja II, who ruled a century after the peak of Rajaraja I and Rajendra I.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): Only 2 and 3 wrongly states that the temple honours Vishnu. It is dedicated to Shiva, and statement 1 on Rajaraja II is true, so this option is wrong.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): Only 1 and 3 accepts the wrong deity and drops the location statement. Darasuram lies in the Tanjore region, so statement 2 must be included.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): 1, 2 and 3 would require the temple to be a Vishnu shrine. As a Shiva temple, it makes statement 3 false and the combination incorrect.

question: The Kampaharesvara temple at Tribhuvanam is an example of the architecture of which period?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Later Chola period.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Kampaharesvara temple at Tribhuvanam is an example of the later Chola temples (कंपहरेश्वर मंदिर, तिरुभुवनम् — उत्तरकालीन चोल कला)

 

• It carries the tradition of the Dravidian style, with the prominent vimana, into the closing phase of the dynasty.

 

• It is listed in the notes after the Tanjore, Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram temples.

 

• It is linked with the reign of Kulottunga III, a king of the later period.

 

• The temple belongs to the closing phase of Chola art, when new buildings were smaller than the giant temples of Rajaraja I and Rajendra I.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Chola art includes both temples and bronzes.

 

• The late Chola phase followed the peak of Rajaraja I and Rajendra I.

 

• The dynasty ended with Rajendra III.

 

• Tribhuvanam is a town near Kumbakonam, and the temple there is dedicated to Shiva as Kampahareswara, the remover of fear.

 

• The temple's tall vimana carries sculpture of great skill and is remembered as one of the last great monuments of the Chola age.

 

NOTE

 

• Pallava period (Option 1): Pallava architecture is represented by the Shore Temple and the Seven Rathas at Mamallapuram, and it came before the Cholas. Tribhuvanam does not belong to that tradition.

 

• Rashtrakuta period (Option 2): Rashtrakuta architecture is best known from the Kailasa temple at Ellora in the Deccan. It was not a Tamil-country style, so Tribhuvanam does not belong to it.

 

• Early Chalukya period (Option 4): Early Chalukya architecture of Badami and Aihole developed in Karnataka in the 6th-8th centuries. The Tribhuvanam temple lies in the Chola country and is much later.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Brihadeshwara temple at Tanjore:

1. It is dedicated to Shiva.

2. It is also known as the Rajarajeswara temple.

3. It was built by Rajendra I.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the Brihadeshwara (Rajarajeswara) temple at Tanjore is dedicated to Shiva (बृहदीश्वर या राजराजेश्वर मंदिर — शिव को समर्पित)

 

• Statement 3 is wrong because it was built by Rajaraja I in 1010 AD, and not by his son Rajendra I.

 

• Rajendra I built the separate Siva temple at Gangaikondacholapuram.

 

• The temple's vimana and Nandimandapa make it the finest example of the Dravidian style.

 

• The temple's alternative name makes it easy to remember the builder, since Rajarajeswara literally means the lord of Rajaraja.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The temple is also called the Big Temple.

 

• It is located in the Kaveri delta.

 

• Most Chola temples were devoted to Shiva.

 

• The temple at Tanjore also has a huge monolithic Nandi facing the sanctum, which is one of the largest such statues in India.

 

• The temple was completed in the year 1010 AD, and it remains in worship, which is why it is called a living temple.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Only 2 and 3 wrongly gives Rajendra I the credit, even though the temple is the work of his father. Statement 1 on the dedication to Shiva is correct, so this fails.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): Only 1 and 3 includes the false builder claim and drops the alternative name. The name Rajarajeswara itself points to Rajaraja I as the builder.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): 1, 2 and 3 cannot be correct because the third statement is false. The son built a different temple at his new capital.
